archetype.name: Pocket Passer (vertical)
archetype.definition: A 36-year-old who wins from the pocket with anticipation and accuracy past ten yards, holds the ball to let routes develop, and no longer adds anything as a runner.

report.headline: Seattle-era downfield accuracy is back, but sacks and the red zone stall drives
report.take:
Geno Smith's 2026 looks more like his 2022-24 Seattle seasons than last year's Raiders slide. His 0.093 EPA per dropback ranks 19th of 49, his 8.09 adjusted net yards per dropback ranks 12th, and his CPOE is up 2.5 points on 2025. That is a quarterback who is a real asset on a per-throw basis. The 2-7 record says more about the defense around him (30th in pass EPA allowed) and the drives he can't finish than about the throws he makes.

The engine is the ball traveling past the sticks. His throws of 10+ air yards have added 62.8 EPA; everything under 10 adds 15.7. The 31 deep attempts at 1.194 EPA each, with a 17.5 CPOE, are the best single trait in the profile. Garrett Wilson (24.7 EPA on 64 targets) and Omar Cooper Jr. (0.865 per target) have been the main beneficiaries. The cost is the 2.92-second time to throw: a 9.4% sack rate ranks 39th, and 35.4% of his pressures become sacks. He is pressured on only a middling 22.1% of dropbacks. He scrambles on just 3.8% of them and his designed runs are a dead loss, so the extended plays aren't paying for the sacks the way a mobile quarterback's would.

The numbers hide two things. First, the sacks land in the worst places: 14 on third down, where he converts only 33.7% facing an average of 8.3 yards, and 7 in the red zone, where his EPA falls to -0.259. A vertical passer loses his best weapon when the field shrinks. Second, the 1.1% interception rate (12th) is not who he has been. He ranked 56th, 46th, 58th and 63rd in interceptions over his last four full seasons. With four turnover-worthy fumbles on top, the clean ball security is the part most likely to give back.

The weekly results split almost entirely by opponent. He posted +10.9, +12.2 and +11.7 EPA against Detroit, Miami and Las Vegas, defenses that now rank 30th, 32nd and 28th. Against Chicago, Cleveland and Kansas City, all top-11 units, he went negative and the bad-throw rate spiked. He is a quarterback who punishes weak coverage rather than one who elevates a struggling team. Without Wilson, even that edge narrows.

strengths.title: Accuracy and production past ten yards
strengths.body: His tenPlus throws carry the offense: a 12.5 CPOE and 0.827 EPA per attempt there. He hit 4 TDs deep against 2 interceptions. This fits what he did in 2022-24, when he ranked 3rd, 17th and 6th in CPOE, so the skill is real. The deep-ball efficiency on 31 attempts will cool, but it won't vanish.

strengths.title: Efficiency rebound from 2025
strengths.body: After a -0.1 EPA per play season with Las Vegas, he is back near his Seattle baseline. His yards per attempt are up nearly a full yard on last year, and his CPOE gain is just as large. The underlying accuracy is ranked solidly in the league's top half. The rebound tracks his best seasons rather than a fluky stretch.

strengths.title: Quality short-to-intermediate game
strengths.body: Beyond the deep shots, his 0-9 throws produce a 54% success rate at 0.177 EPA. The 10-19 window adds 0.573 EPA with a 9.1 CPOE. The screen and swing game behind the line of scrimmage is the only depth that loses value.

concerns.title: Sacks that kill third downs
concerns.body: The 9.4% sack rate is the price of holding the ball for downfield routes. Without scrambling to offset it, it is a real cost rather than a neutral trade. Fourteen of his 28 sacks came on third down, which is why his third-down EPA is negative despite a 6.7 CPOE there. His pressure-to-sack rate has swung between 22% and 46% over the past four years, so expect this to persist at roughly this level.

concerns.title: Red zone and late-game stalls
concerns.body: In the red zone his EPA drops to -0.259 on a 52.8% completion rate, with 7 sacks in a compressed field. That's why his TD rate ranks just 27th despite top-half efficiency. Close fourth quarters (-0.185) follow the same pattern, and it helps explain a 2-7 record alongside positive passing EPA.

concerns.title: Interception rate due to rise
concerns.body: His 1.1% interception rate sits well below his history: he finished 58th of 60 in interceptions in 2024 and last of 63 in 2025. Over the last three games it is already up to 2.1%. Pair that with four lost-or-worthy fumbles, and turnovers are the likeliest source of slippage.

trend.note: The game-by-game line follows the opponent. He posted three straight double-digit EPA outings against bottom-five defenses in Weeks 3, 7 and 8, and negative games against Chicago, Cleveland and Kansas City. The last three average a better EPA per dropback than his season. The last five average a worse one.

nextGame.headline: No Garrett Wilson, but Buffalo's offense should force volume
nextGame.body:
Buffalo's defense is middle of the pack: 16th in pass EPA allowed and 15th on short throws. It is better against the deep ball (9th), which is where Smith makes his money. Its 3rd-ranked hit rate is a problem for a quarterback who holds the ball and turns pressure into sacks, though the Bills' 21st-ranked sack rate suggests they get home less often than they hit. Buffalo's offense ranks 3rd in EPA against a Jets pass defense ranked 30th, and the Book has the Jets as 8.5-point underdogs with a 50.5 total. That points to a trailing script and plenty of attempts. His EPA when down 9 or more (0.189) has held up fine.

The availability that matters is his own receiver room. Garrett Wilson is out with a concussion, and Wilson is his most-targeted receiver and his biggest EPA source. That pushes Adonai Mitchell into the WR1 role and Omar Cooper Jr. into more snaps. On Buffalo's side, left tackle Dion Dawkins is out. That bears on Smith only through game flow: a weaker Bills line is one of the few things that could keep this from becoming a shootout he is chasing.

keyMatchups.title: Adonai Mitchell as the new WR1
keyMatchups.body: Mitchell has been efficient at 0.378 EPA per target in the No. 2 role. Buffalo has let WR1s score 5.3 PPR points over their averages, 30th of 32, while holding WR2s well under. If Mitchell inherits the top role cleanly, the soft spot in this defense lines up with him.

keyMatchups.title: Hit rate versus time to throw
keyMatchups.body: Buffalo hits quarterbacks at the league's third-highest rate. Smith's 2.92-second average gives that rush time to arrive. His worst games came when pressure spiked, like the 44.4% pressured day in Chicago.

keyMatchups.title: Shootout script and Cooper's role
keyMatchups.body: With Buffalo's 3rd-ranked passing offense facing the Jets' 30th-ranked pass defense, Smith likely needs volume and chunk plays. Cooper has been the most explosive option per target. Buffalo's defense also funnels an above-normal share of targets to running backs, which suits checkdowns if the rush wins.

nextGame.watch: Whether Smith keeps taking intermediate and deep shots to Mitchell and Cooper without Wilson, or retreats to checkdowns and sacks as he did against Kansas City.

restOfSeason.body:
The accuracy and downfield production are sustainable: they match three Seattle seasons and have held up across nine starts. The deep-ball rate on 31 attempts will not stay this high, though, and the interception rate is likely to drift toward his career norm. I'd expect efficiency to settle closer to average-plus than top-12. Volume should stay steady with a defense that can't get stops, and sacks will keep arriving at about three a game.

I project roughly 215-255 passing yards a game with 1.1-1.6 TDs and 0.6-1.0 interceptions. The range leans on two things. One is how long Wilson is out: his return date is listed as an estimate. The other is how many of the remaining opponents resemble the weak defenses he shredded rather than the top-11 units that held him negative.

confidence.note: The efficiency fits his career, but the deep-ball sample is small and Wilson's absence reshapes the targets.
